h: Cairns, Stones and a Short Hop to the Past
p: Out on the field, look out for the tall memorial cairn, put up in 1881, and the Well of the Dead, where tradition says a wounded Highland chief fell. The headstones naming the clans were added at the same time as the cairn, and many visitors find a stone with their own surname. Every April, around the anniversary of the battle, people gather here to remember, so expect it to be busier and more emotional then.

Allow around two hours to do the exhibition and a decent walk of the moor without rushing. If you have time left, the Clava Cairns are only a short drive away. These Bronze Age burial cairns and standing stones sit in a peaceful grove of trees and are free to wander round, a striking contrast with the battlefield's open moor. You'll pass close to the great Culloden railway viaduct over the River Nairn too.
For a bigger dose of Jacobite history, Fort George at Ardersier, built after the rising to keep the Highlands in check, is a short drive north-east and still a working army base.
